Moreover, there was no difference in rate of ventilator-associated mortality between ranitidine and sucralfate recipients. A further meta-analysis21 has in turn raised doubts about the efficacy of ranitidine; no significant benefit was found for ranitidine, compared with placebo, in the prevention of bleeding. One clinical guideline suggests that, given the conflicting evidence, the choice between antacids, H2- antagonists, and sucralfate be made on an institutional basis.16 PPIs are also used for stress ulcer prophylaxis, al- though the evidence base for such use is lacking.17 Bleeding ulcer. Peptic ulceration is responsible for about 50% of all cases of upper gastrointestinal bleeding: the condition is potentially life-threatening and in severe cases prompt resuscitation with intravenous fluids and blood may be required. About 80% of patients will stop bleeding spontaneously without recurrence, but the remaining 20% are at risk of severe morbidity or death,22 and early strati- fication into low- and high-risk categories on the basis of clinical and endoscopic criteria is important for proper management.22,23 No treatment may be needed for low- risk patients, but those with a clot in an ulcer bed should undergo irrigation and appropriate treatment of the under- lying lesion, and high-risk patients should be given imme- diate endoscopic injection therapy for haemostasis.22 Many different solutions have been used for endoscopic injection, including adrenaline (alone or with sclerosants such as monoethanolamine or lauromacrogol), alcohol, fibrin glue, sodium tetradecyl sulfate, thrombin, or saline (normal or hypertonic); none has been clearly shown to be superior.22 Adrenaline injection will achieve haemostasis in up to 95% of patients although bleeding will recur in up to 20% of these; there is little evidence that addition of sclerosants reduces the rate of rebleeding, and their use may lead to life-threatening necrosis of the injected area.23 Thermal, laser, or multipolar (coaptive) or plasma electro- coagulative endoscopic techniques are also of benefit, and again there is no clear evidence to prefer one over anoth- er.22 Combining injection with thermal coagulation may be of greater benefit than either alone; UK guidelines con- sider it may be better in a subset of patients with active arterial bleeding, although it is not considered to offer ad- ditional benefit in most patients,23 while subsequent Cana- dian guidelines consider the combination superior.22 The use of mechanical clips may also be effective,22,23 espe- cially for active
